In this study, a detailed analysis is conducted on the predicted signatures associated with the primordial black hole phenomenon, focusing specifically on the influence imposed by spherical symmetry breakdowns. Using 30 models describing the breakdown of this symmetry, we compute the maximum gravitational wave frequency and the orbital period at the moment of the supposed big bang, in addition to the mass of the black holes and the distances between them at that time. A majority of these systems, in fact, form within the estimated age of the universe at just a few hundred million years after the cosmic big bang. Moreover, our findings reveal significant variations in the predicted gravitational wave signals, in terms of amplitude and spectral distribution, which enable us to distinguish between the various models describing the breakdown of spherical symmetry. In particular, our results show a range of approximately 1.3 to 16 times more gravitational energy emitted two weeks before the supposed primordial black hole formation, in contrast to the standard spherical model. A variety of structural models, which determine the distribution of matter within these black holes, are also considered, in addition to the predicted gravitational wave signals. In particular, our findings show a less intense gravitational signal, in terms of amplitude, for these models compared to the standard spherical model. In any case, detecting these signals poses a considerable challenge for current and future detectors, such as LIGO and its upgraded versions. In contrast, space-based detectors, such as LISA, may potentially explore the parameter space associated with various models describing the breakdown of spherical symmetry. In particular, distinguishing between models with a moderate breakdown of symmetry may be possible using a selection of detectors that detect signals from these black holes at different frequencies, such as LISA and ground-based second-generation detectors like KAGRA and other upcoming projects. In summary, our study provides valuable insights into the potential exploration of theoretical models describing the formation and properties of primordial black holes through gravitational wave detection. In particular, distinguishing between models describing the breakdown of spherical symmetry appears to be a feasible goal, and we anticipate that space-based detectors, in collaboration with ground-based second-generation detectors, will play a significant role in this research. isy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, face several technical limitations, hindering their performance in large-scale applications. To overcome these limitations, developing strategies to optimize available quantum resources is a necessity. A promising approach to expand the utility of quantum computers is found in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs), which, despite their efficiency, are susceptible to suboptimal results due to overparameterization. Overparameterization not only hampers the accuracy of these algorithms, but it also complicates the process of achieving convergence. In this research, a novel regulatory framework inspired by the L1 and L2 regularizations widely used in classical machine learning is proposed to counter overparameterization in VQAs. The suggested method, known as the L1-L2 Quantum Regularization (L1-L2Q) framework, integrates both low-level quantum hardware and high-level artificial intelligence techniques to minimize noise arising from quantum operations. To facilitate practical applications, this framework is implemented using Python and run on a Fujitsu Quantum Computing device. The framework's effectiveness is evaluated by its ability to prevent overtraining in the context of a quantum machine learning algorithm where it regulates the parameters of a Perceptron-based classifier. The implemented L1-L2Q framework significantly prevents overtraining, achieving robust generalization beyond the training data, and thereby demonstrating an evident suppression of noise in the quantum circuit. Moreover, our analysis reveals a correlation between the prevention of overtraining and the inherent properties of the quantum superposition principle. The L1-L2Q framework's performance also indicates an obvious improvement in convergence time, which aligns with the expectations from the algorithm based on the principle of quantum adaptation. The suggested L1-L2Q framework is anticipated to facilitate the large-scale deployment of quantum computing and thereby accelerate advancements towards quantum AI. The implementation of this framework is publicly available on the Fujitsu Quantum Community forum. Similar approaches to quantum machine learning could greatly benefit from the integration of this regulatory framework. Furthermore, due to the emerging nature of quantum hardware, this L1-L2Q framework is well-positioned to address overparameterization issues common in NISQ quantum hardware and software applications. Neural Networks, have benefited from the inclusion of uncertainty in state and action estimation for robotics. However, traditional BNN training is hindered by a limited selection of data, mainly due to the expense associated with generating simulations. Consequently, standard training methods fall short in generating diverse data sets. In response, this study presents two innovative methods that broaden the scope of data for training Bayesian Neural Networks through the integration of real-world data rectification and the application of a generative model. The first approach involves leveraging real-world data to construct distributions that accurately represent the relationships within the training data, thus filling knowledge gaps. The second method utilizes a generative model to produce simulations based on learned distributions, ensuring simulations accurately reflect real-world data. The proposed techniques are successfully demonstrated in a dataset extraction task, where the incorporation of real-world data and simulation data trained with the newly proposed methods resulted in significantly enhanced uncertainty representation when compared to a traditional training approach. Additionally, a novel uncertainty visualization technique, Uncertainty Sphere, was introduced to facilitate understanding of the learned uncertainty by comparing it to the training distribution. The use of these new methods has led to substantial improvements in state and action estimation accuracy. Furthermore, the ensembles trained with the proposed methods exhibited resilience to out-of-distribution data, as validated by testing against various datasets extraction tasks. The analysis demonstrated that neural network ensembles are capable of adapting to diverse data trained with the proposed methods, thereby increasing the diversity of data in robotics tasks and subsequent applications, including visual navigation and navigation in unknown environments. The experiments conducted revealed significant gains in uncertainty representation when the diversity of data is increased, leading to enhanced state and action estimation accuracy. The novel Uncertainty Sphere visualization tool facilitates the assessment of uncertainty by comparing it to the training distribution, thus enabling deeper understanding of the learned uncertainty. The proposed methods have the potential to be applied in various robotics tasks and subsequent applications, including out-of-distribution data, navigation in unknown environments, visual navigation, and more. For instance, there have been several reported cases of cyberbullying that ultimately
led to tragic consequences. Despite efforts to address this problem, detecting the
form of online harassment an individual experiences remains a major challenge.
This study delves into the sub-field of cyberbullying detection, focusing on the
detection of types of online harassment. We examine the current state of cyberbullying
research and analysis, highlighting the difficulties in identifying the form of
online harassment an individual experiences. We also explore the most effective
features in machine learning models, enabling more accurate harassment detection
in the future. Building on previous studies employing text preprocessing methods,
this research investigates the efficiency of supervised learning without pre-processing
the text. For this purpose, a novel dataset, known as EM-DATA, was created by
merging five existing bullying datasets and utilizing them for training and testing
purposes. A comparative analysis of various algorithms was conducted using different
features, and the outcomes in the context of explicit and implied harassment
are presented. Furthermore, exploratory analysis of word2vec vectors revealed the
importance of specific words in classifying the two types of cyberbullying. 
Ultimately, the interplay of cyberbullying detection, its related research, and
the analysis presented in this study are discussed. Specifically, the study identifies
the most effective features, the importance of using existing labels to train models,
the enhancement of existing datasets, and potential future research directions. 
Additionally, the outcomes of the comparative analysis are presented in the context
of explicit and implied harassment, and the feasibility of using machine learning
models to detect these types of cyberbullying is demonstrated. As a result, the study
achieved an 86% high-f1 score in the classification of explicit harassment and
an 81% high-f1 score in the classification of implied harassment. The study, however,
experienced a decline in performance when cross-validation was conducted. A deeper
analysis of the data reveals that a substantial proportion of the data is composed
of ambiguous text that does not accurately classify either explicit or implied
harassment. Consequently, the study suggests an increase in the size of the training
dataset by including this type of ambiguous data to improve the classification
of the underrepresented group. Ultimately, the study's outcomes serve as a foundation
for further research in the area of cyberbullying classification. Based on the study's
outcomes, the potential research directions for future studies are identified.

of a recently developed antiferromagnet, Yb2In2Li2, which exhibits a unique triangular structure. In-depth studies of specific heat and magnetic enthalpy through direct crystal probe measurement revealed the specific heat capacity of Yb2In2Li2 to be 0.054 J/K^2 per mole, indicating no anomaly associated with the spin-1/2 insulating state of the Yb3+ ions, and confirming that the system has no charge transfer between the Yb2+ and In3+ ions. Measurements conducted on a magnetic field of up to 14 Tesla revealed two well-defined anomalies at 0.58 Tesla and 5.15 Tesla. These results correspond to the two individual Yb2+ spin flips within a unique low-energy regime characterized by a spin-1 effective state of the local moment. Finite temperature susceptibility measurements provided additional evidence for this 0.58 Tesla and 5.15 Tesla magnetic field, supporting the two-state model via a time-averaged effective Hamiltonian. Furthermore, temperature-dependent measurements of the magnetic enthalpy revealed two phases at 0.37 K and 0.58 K, indicating two successive spin-freeze temperatures. Finally, theoretical studies using a virtual crystal approximation in combination with a unique effective Hamiltonian, taking into consideration the time-averaged behavior of the local moment, successfully reproduced the principal experimental findings, thereby validating the theoretical approach and Hamiltonian. This overall combination of experimental and theoretical analysis has allowed for an in-depth determination of the low-temperature magnetic phases of Yb2In2Li2 to be 0.37 K and 0.58 K, and for an understanding of the unique low-energy regime characterized by a spin-1 effective state of the local moment. These results may have a significant impact on the search for, and interpretation of, quasiparticle behavior within insulating state matter in quantum magnets. This study has brought into sharp focus two fundamental concepts in the field of quantum magnetism: (1) the occurrence of spin-state mixing that leads to a unique effective spin-1 state; (2) the establishment of the first theoretical model for a time-averaged effective Hamiltonian in the context of insulating state matter in quantum magnets. This successful application of a virtual crystal approximation in conjunction with a unique effective Hamiltonian, specifically designed to model spin-1 behavior within a nearest neighbor spin interaction, has provided invaluable insight into the nature of the low-temperature magnetic phases of Yb2In2Li2

This research implements a quantum version of the Rabin-Karp algorithm using the quantum random oracle model. The approach replaces traditional hash functions with quantum ones, yielding better performance. The results show that with $m$ characters in the input string and a desired quantum failure probability of $\varepsilon$, a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(2^m/\varepsilon)$ and space complexity of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ can be achieved, providing a quantum speedup over classical variants when $m$ is large and $\varepsilon$ is small. The approach works by employing a set of quantum hash functions based on the quantum version of the ideal hash function proposed by Indyk. These functions are used in conjunction with a classical post-processing step to improve the overall performance. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes neural networks to predict the deformation of the avatar model based on the movement data obtained. increasingly significant in natural language processing: vocabulary reduction and text simplification. Vocabulary reduction, a technique employed in natural language simulation and generation, involves deliberately limiting the vocabulary available for text generation to produce concise, high-quality text. This is contrasted with text simplification, which is a well-studied topic but can be challenging due to the inherent difficulty of assessing the ease of understanding of written text. Our discussion of vocabulary reduction will cover its applications and techniques, along with a focus on its connection to text simplification. We will also examine methods for evaluating and simplifying text using various metrics for measuring text comprehensibility. Furthermore, we will explore techniques for simplifying text, particularly those utilizing pre-trained language models, parallel data, and pre-trained embeddings. Additionally, we will delve into methods for selecting and reducing vocabulary. Our goal is to provide readers with a comprehensive understanding of these essential topics in natural language processing. Additionally, we intend to highlight avenues for further investigation, which appear underrepresented in the current literature. Lastly, we will summarise the results of the 2021 and 2022 Text Simplification Workshops, which were a source of motivation for our work.  Due to the overlapping themes between vocabulary reduction and text simplification, we will treat these topics as interconnected domains, allowing us to present the material in a unified manner. Consequently, we will frequently cross-reference between the two topics, rather than presenting the material in a strictly segregated fashion. As a result, this presentation will showcase the reciprocal influence between vocabulary reduction and text simplification, which we believe is a beneficial approach.  The remainder of this introduction provides a brief overview of each topic before examining their interconnection and relevance to natural language processing. Vocabulary reduction, in contrast to text simplification, has a more modest history in natural language processing, with the majority of applications found in natural language simulation and generation. This is, however, a perfect time to explore this topic since recent advancements in the capacity of language models have made it more feasible to deliberately restrict the vocabulary and produce high-quality text. This is particularly true for applications in which highly specialized or domain-specific vocabulary is prevalent, such as in the simulating the behavior of individuals who possess a limited vocabulary due to learning disabilities or poverty. As for text simplification, numerous techniques have been employed to assess and improve the ease of understanding of written text. Our discussion, however, will concentrate on methods that are specifically designed to simplify pre-connected pairs of sentences, which originate from various domains such as science, medicine, and education

By combining the benefits of height-based and distance-based models, our approach incorporates the impacts of topography, non-uniform wind, and multiple fire sources into a single prediction model. We have adapted the Green Blanket model to address the challenges of simulating multiple fire behaviors, and incorporated the Haines-DeBraal spread equation to mimic real-fire behavior. Additionally, our framework utilizes the Simple Iterative Improvement method to optimize the fire spread simulation. Validation of our model was performed using a benchmark 256x256 Utah Valley map and a larger 4096x4096 real-world heightmap map, showcasing successful results and a notable improvement in performance over previous implementations. We believe this model, combined with an advanced forest management model, could accurately simulate the effects of preventing and combating forest fires. Finally, we have released the full forest fire simulator source code under an open-source license to facilitate further community development and research.  In terms of the simulation efficiency, our model achieves substantial improvement over the prior Max-Flow implementation, achieving a notable speed-up of approximately 5-10 times when using the same heightmap data, and reaching near-real-time performance when utilizing multi-threading and GPU acceleration techniques. However, it is worth noting that achieving real-time performance for large maps with complex heightmap data, such as a full real-world map, would likely require the use of more advanced parallel processing techniques and a potential model redesign. Nonetheless, our code provides a solid foundation for further optimization and community development.  In conclusion, our model succeeds in incorporating the effects of terrain into a forest fire propagation simulation, and we achieve a notable improvement in performance over the prior Max-Flow implementation. However, we recognize that our model may still fall short of the ideal accuracy compared to the existing height-based forest fire propagation models, and we are exploring the integration of additional relevant sensory data, such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed, to enhance the simulation realism. Furthermore, we are investigating the integration of advanced computer vision techniques to automate the fire detection process and improve the simulation accuracy. Ultimately, we believe our code has significant potential for development and research in the field of forest fire simulation and prevention.  In terms of future research potential, our model opens up several avenues for further investigation, and we are confident that our code will facilitate a multi-disciplinary approach to the development of forest fire simulation. However, being a black-box approach, training a large-scale CSI-to-location mapping is a significant challenge when considering limited observation data and latent variables.  In this research, a novel localization approach based on deep neural networks is proposed for wireless localization using channel state information (WLSI).  To facilitate effective localization, a deep latent mapping technique is designed to reveal the underlying latent variables representing location information, followed by a procedure called latent utility learning that identifies location-related latent variables and a subsequent model that maps CSI to location information.  Moreover, this research proves the existence of latent variables in the network and provides theoretical support for the proposed method.  To facilitate practical implementation, a simplified model is proposed to concurrently train multiple latent variables, and experimental results verify the efficiency and superiority of the proposed model.  Compared to conventional DNNs, the proposed model exhibits improved localization accuracy and reduced input dependence on irrelevant location latent variables.  Notably, the proposed model is compatible with various wireless localization techniques.  With this knowledge, a novel weight prediction model called LW2P is proposed to estimate the weight matrices of deep latent utility models during deployment, eliminating the requirement for large-scale calibration.  Finally, an uncertainty analysis via sensitivity testing proves the robustness of the proposed model.  Notably, the potential uncertainty in the latent utility model estimated by LW2P affects the final localization result's accuracy and accuracy-discordance trade-off.  Investigating the initial uncertainty of the deep latent utility model reveals the difficulty in initially learning this model under certain circumstances and the potential solution by incorporating extra out-of-vocabulary (inconvenient locations) to aid localization.  Consequently, this research proposes a novel data preparation technique to facilitate effective localization and reduce initial uncertainty, and experimental results verify the improved localization accuracy and reduced uncertainty.  With this knowledge, a novel localization approach called WLSI$^2$ is proposed and involves two phases: the first is to prepare a set of convenient data for initialization and demonstration purposes and the second is to develop a novel model called ConLUMBER that specifically handles out-of-vocabulary (inconvenient location) localizations within the same family (e.g. indoor-to-indoor) and shows potential in achieving a zero-discordance accuracy result with adequate training data.  Finally, the feasibility of the proposed technique is tested in a simulated 3D indoor environment featuring multiple rooms.

This paper evaluates two modes of programming: instant execution and compilation. We conducted surveys and gathered feedback from over 350 students who experienced both instant execution and compilation, aiming to identify the preferences of each group and understand how students perceive the learning process with each method. Our study revealed distinct views on collaboration, feedback, and error correction under both conditions, yet no clear winners in terms of performance based on the standard metrics for student success. Thorough analysis of the data uncovered that students using instant execution tend to struggle more with the concept of code modification and the importance of feedback and error correction. Conversely, compilation users often prioritize code beauty over functionality. These findings highlight the significance of the feedback loop in the learning process and encourage instructors to emphasize algorithmic quality and the impact of code changes, regardless of the environment used. As programming education becomes more diverse, understanding how students respond to various contexts could lead to tailored interventions to improve learning outcomes. This study lays the groundwork for exploring other environments that could optimize student performance. Our approach to philosophy is characterized by focusing on the relationships between these concepts, rather than exploring their individual manifestations in various areas of legal theory. This methodology allows us to identify three distinct phases of reflection on law and norm, each of which is marked by a particular understanding of the connection between these concepts. The first phase encompasses traditional legal theory, where law is viewed as a subset of norm, with norms categorized into legal and non-legal varieties. The second phase is represented by contemporary legal theory, where the relationship between law and norm is seen as more complex, with norms dependent on other norms, particularly those associated with social norms, for existence and validity. In the third phase, which is characterized by a more recent and nuanced perspective, the connection between law and norm takes on a more dynamic and dialectical quality, with norms influenced by laws and vice versa. This approach to the subject is distinct from existing three-phased accounts of law, as it focuses on the relationships between these concepts rather than individual concepts themselves. Furthermore, our classification system is flexible, with the possibility of existing entities that do not fit into the three phases, as well as a potential fourth phase, where the distinction between law and norm is simply a matter of fact, rather than a matter of logical relationship. Finally, our analysis raises questions about the completeness of our classification system, as well as the task of identifying the correct phase of legal theory for particular existing approaches. This classification can serve as a starting point for further discussion, with the potential for existing theories to be reinterpreted in terms of the three phases, as well as the possibility of new theories emerging that highlight the connection between law and norm. Given that these attacks require specialized equipment to fabricate the patches, which is unlikely to be on hand by malicious agents, a long-standing concern has been whether such attacks can be executed with the same hardware used to capture the target images. This study confirms the feasibility of delivering successful patch-based attacks on images taken with a standard smartphone camera, making malicious agents a more formidable threat. Nonetheless, employing physical world adversarial patches on mobile devices poses some distinct difficulties. Because patches block part of the target image, which may be a portion of the label, the attack may fail if the patch obstructs crucial image information. Moreover, as patches are uniform, they should cover multiple standard OTS (off-the-shelf) patches, keeping the cost of the attack low. Our proposed method, called patchcon, optimizes the design of the adversarial patch, which is a combination of uniform noise and a sample from the target class. Our results show that patchcon significantly outperforms previous methods, achieving a success rate of 59.1% (57.1%) on smartphones with patch sizes of 20/35 pixels. Importantly, our attack is the first to explicitly handle the misclassification caused by partial target image occlusion, as well as the one-sided loss used in existing methods. Compared to the state-of-the-art attack, our proposal requires, on average, 6.7 (5.8) times fewer iterations to find a successful patch when using a large patch size of 35 (20). This is while achieving a success rate that is, on average, 10.9% (11.6%) higher than the most comparable methods. Interestingly, our results show that incorporating the uniform noise used in many attacks can significantly slow down the attack. As a result, our simple, fast proposal, called fast_patchcon, outperforms patchcon in terms of the number of iterations required. Our study enables us to make concrete, realistic predictions regarding the energy distribution in the femtogram range for the production of electron-positron pairs in various motion scenarios. Moreover, in cases involving just two systems, we demonstrate that the energy losses due to pair production exhibit a universal logarithmic dependence on the minimum momentum scale involved. Our work sets the groundwork for exploring the extension of this analysis to other parameters in subsequent studies. Most existing studies focus on theoretical aspects and provide practical implementations as an afterthought. In this study, we address two critical concerns that must be addressed when integrating stochastic deep learning methods into industry ranking systems: 
    1. Developing stable and consistent serving algorithms that can accurately maintain the learning results, as well as minimizing serving overhead.
    2. Ensuring that the choice of stochastic deep learning objective function doesn't contradict the system's design intent.
    1. We empirically analyzed the behavior of stochastic deep learning methods within a real-world e-commerce search platform and found that despite their ability to achieve comparable performance with less training, they all failed to meet at least one critical ranking system requirement.
    2. We developed, tested, and integrated stable and consistent serving transforms, specifically'stable stochastic ranking' (STAR) and 'temporal STAR' (TSTAR), into our industry search platform, in order to maintain the learning results.
    The integration of stochastic deep learning methods into industry ranking systems is still in its early stages. Leveraging these methods without thorough consideration for the underlying system's design and implementation will continue to lead to challenges. As such, we recommend the incorporation of dedicated researchers and engineers who can bridge the gap between theoretical advancements, implementation details, and industry production deployment. 
    The implementation details and code for stable serving transforms are openly available at https://github.com/Tencent/RRS. 
    The temporary STAR code is available at https://github.com/T-Airym/t-temporal-star. 
    This study was presented at IJCAI 2020. 
    The e-commerce search platform used in this study was a hot product search feature on a popular Chinese website, utilized by over 100 million users per day, with over 100 million items stored within the platform. 
    The study's experiments were conducted using GPU and CPU resources from the Tencent QDS and Microsoft Azure platforms; access to these resources was facilitated through the Nectar cloud portal. 
    The temporal serving transform was inspired by Giuseppe Martina et al.'s work on temporal ranking models and was implemented in collaboration with them at Microsoft. 
    The current study focuses on stochastic deep learning methods; future studies will incorporate other advances in machine learning, e.g., contextual and model-agnostic methods, into the industry ranking system.

This direction-based perspective enables researchers to utilize the concept of 'field-line distance' as a measurable indicator of the overall cross-field transport rate. By combining observations from the High Resolution Imager on board the Fast Scanning Spectroscopic Urbinelli telescope (FSSURVI) with 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we investigate the characteristics of plasma density and vertical velocity across magnetic field lines within regions devoid of polar networks. The results from our studies based on observed tracers indicate an average cross-field transport time of approximately 76 minutes, which corresponds to a transport coefficient of $8.9 \times 10^4$ km$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$. The average transport time in our model simulations ranges between 33-77 minutes, which falls within the same order of magnitude as the observed value. Furthermore, these transport times align with those derived from numerical simulations using different models over the past two decades. The differences in observed and simulated transport times can be attributed to the overall atmospheric pressure variations. This study provides the initial direct comparison between the rates obtained from observational and numerical studies to date. The implications of our research are that observational signatures of cross-field transport may manifest as a temporal increase in the emission line intensity across the entire range of magnetic field strengths, particularly within the upper chromosphere where the plasma and magnetic field separations exhibit the largest variations. Nevertheless, our predictions based on the observed transport time yield slightly lower density enhancements compared to the levels seen in the chromosphere. The predicted intensity maxima may be observable using the Sr II 1335.220 nm line but may be at the detection limits for the Na I 669.3 nm line; we recommend the use of the FSSURVI's spectral mode to increase our understanding of the atmospheric dynamics. Traditionally, GPUs have followed the standard sequence of fit (estimating model parameters) and evaluate (making predictions) steps in a learning process. However, doing so can lead to inefficient performance for real-time learning, where prediction demands constant interruption during the training cycle. In response, we introduce the concept of learn-evaluate-integrate (LEI), a novel approach that unites the fit and evaluate functions on GPUs through a functional programming framework. This method constructs a continuous flow where the model is refined with each prediction outcome, eliminating the need for distinct fit and evaluate operations. The LEI technique is further optimized by combining prediction calculations into batches, thus reducing communication between the GPU and CPU. Experimental results demonstrate that LEI-based algorithms are equally effective as their traditional counterparts both on GPUs and in distributed settings, with the added benefit of real-time parallelization and enhanced GPU performance in high-speed networks. Moreover, the distributed LEI model is scalable, linear in terms of system resources and increases efficiency by up to 72% in certain scenarios. By incorporating deep learning capabilities, we have achieved comparable accuracy with shallow learning methods while also achieving significant speedup - up to 91% on GPUs. The LEI framework offers a flexible framework for instantiating various machine learning and neural network techniques using the REVEAL programming library, allowing for a wide range of algorithms to be integrated and improved. The LEI technique, specifically its linear distribution and GPU processing, can also be applied to other machine learning methods, leading to increased efficiency and speed. The LEI-based computational flow is further explored as a potential solution for real-time complex system design problems, offering a new approach to concurrent model training and prediction operations. The addition of neural networks, specifically, results in superior accuracy with the LEI-based method. The integration of LEI into graphics processing units not only accelerates processing but also enables computation of complex event sequences, translating into predictions of future system states based on past observations. This study examines how AI-based matchmaking can improve career opportunities for applicants by presenting relevant job postings in a more accurate and accessible order. To evaluate the benefits, we developed a comprehensive performance metric that compares the performance of AI-powered matching against alternative search methods, including random job selection and algorithms based on the applicant's previous work experience. Our analysis, using a large dataset of over 240,000 job ads and more than 54,000 user profiles from a mock-up online platform, reveals significant advantages to users. According to the results, AI-based matching leads to up to 25% more relevant job opportunities being displayed to users compared to traditional methods, and users can find suitable job openings approximately 3 times faster. Furthermore, AI-based matching also yields a 66% reduction in the number of job openings that are unlikely to be suitable for the user, thus saving user time and increasing the accuracy of the matching process. To substantiate the practical effectiveness of the proposed AI-based matching algorithm, this study employs a comprehensive metric that combines accuracy, user experience, and computational complexity, thereby bridging traditional trade-offs between relevance and accessibility, and ensuring that the algorithm is reliable and efficient. Experimental comparisons with alternative algorithms confirm that our approach results in substantial user benefit. The study of asteroid physical properties and shapes is crucial in understanding their cosmic origins, internal structures, and surface features. This study applies the Ursa Minor catalog-based approach to 28,934 asteroids from the Lowell database to derive photometric parameters including albedos, diameters, and shapes. The resulting parameters are compared with prevailing benchmarks, and any discrepancies are addressed. The use of the Ursa Minor catalog significantly enhances the recovery of true shapes, breaking the degeneracy associated with traditional fitting methods, and its performance is demonstrated to be superior to the traditional methods. The resulting asteroid datasets are characterized by notable density and shape consistency and exhibit substantial correlations with existing data points. Although this study is limited to small asteroids due to the characteristics of the Ursa Minor catalog, the recovery of diameters and shapes is impressive, and further research is needed to extend this approach to larger asteroids. The resulting data and code used in this study are made publicly available for potential use. The approach leverages radiative transfer models to derive photometric parameters, and future research will explore extending this approach to facilitate astrometry and thermophysical modeling. Ultimately, this study aims to improve understanding of small asteroids through the analysis of samples similar to asteroids 21 Luthenia and 288 Glauke. The resulting parameters are density values ranging from 650 to 2100 kg/m3, and shape consistency values ranging from 0.4 to 0.9. Additionally, notable correlations with larger sets of data points are discovered. Despite constraints associated with the use of the Ursa Minor catalog size, the results provide strong evidence for an optimized set of physical parameters for small asteroids that are consistent with densities observed in the solar system. The approaches used in this study are restricted by the characteristics of the Ursa Minor catalog. Consequently, the recovery of diameters is limited by diameter-range and the shapes are limited by sphere- ellipsoid transition, and further research is necessary to improve these limitations. Nonetheless, the results are found to be consistent with prevailing benchmarks, and the use of the Ursa Minor catalog is found to be an efficient method in recovering photometric parameters of small asteroids compared to the traditional methods. The approaches used in this study are made publicly available as Ursa Minor-LOW, and the resulting data and code are available through the link https://doi.org/10.24414/UrsaMinorLOW1 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icar.2021.04.007

While graph neural networks build models that learn from complex graph features, label propagation spreads label information across neighboring nodes, then combining it for final predictions. As both approaches rely heavily on graph structure, removing or manipulating the neighbors of a node, $v$, significantly impacts both its GNN model and the label propagation process. In the case of GNNs, altering $v$'s features affects its self-loop self-connection; in label propagation, changing $v$'s labels spreads the new label to its neighbors, eventually reaching the node itself. From this understanding, we developed a method called zeroing targets (ZT) which separately modifies these neighbors' self-loops and their corresponding labels during training. Our approach can be widely applied to both GNNs and label propagation since it involves straightforward modifications. Experimental results show that our ZT method notably enhances both GNNs and label propagation while also revealing intriguing connections between these methods and semi-supervised learning schemes. Moreover, our ZT method was found to significantly improve the robustness of GNNs and label propagation against random attacks and also increase their robustness against strategic, malicious attacks when compared to baseline removal methods. We also discovered that our ZT method can serve as a robust proxy to assess the impact of removing nodes in graphs like social networks, Facebook, Twitter, and the human brain's neural network, and also enhance the performance of hybrid GNN-label propagation algorithms when integrated into semi-supervised learning schemes. compiler optimization that involves customizing basic block instructions to exploit hardware features like tailoring TLBs and caches to a specific microarchitecture. Current instruction tuning methods have limitations, particularly in how they apply fine-grained, transitive speculative control dependencies across basic blocks. Despite these limitations, recent studies have shown that considering such dependencies can lead to superior-tuned programs with substantial performance gains in various applications. To address this, we have developed a novel approach called SpecTune, which focuses on tuning conditional instructions by accounting for transitive speculative control dependencies. SpecTune achieves this through the use of 1) tuned instruction groups that enable direct speculation control, 2) tuned instruction sequences that facilitate indirect speculation control, and 3) dependency analysis to optimize speculation, all within a machine-learning-based framework. To evaluate SpecTune, we have developed a diverse set of speculative benchmarks representing varying levels of complexity and control dependencies. Compared to existing tuning methods, SpecTune consistently outperforms them by 15% on average across these benchmarks. Moreover, we have found that SpecTune also provides general low-overhead performance improvements in applications with complex control flows, whereas applying current tuning methods may even degrade performance by up to 13%. This suggests that SpecTune can serve as an essential baseline for future instruction tuning research. SpecTune's full source code is publicly available on GitHub, complemented by the `SpecBench` benchmark suite, which can be accessed at the specified GitHub repository. Similar to other studies in this field, the `SpecBench` suite aims to contribute to the development of benchmarks for evaluating compiler and hardware design strategies. To accommodate a wide range of hardware and software designs, `SpecBench` currently caters to a diverse set of benchmarks representing various program complexity, size, and control flow behaviors. As a result, `SpecBench` offers a suite of simple benchmarks, as well as others that are more challenging, spanning from synthetic benchmarks like `SpecTuneMark1` and `SpecTuneMark2` to real applications like `blackscholes`, `bbq`, and `nn`. To provide a comprehensive evaluation of various design strategies, `SpecBench$-$1` is currently under development and will soon be made publicly available. This initial version of `SpecBench$-$1` is tailored to the RISC-V instruction set architecture and is specifically optimized for 64-bit RISC-V processors, although `SpecBench$-$1` is designed to be easily adapted for other

Active learning is typically used to label data from large, representative datasets. However, when working with imbalanced datasets, this approach can be problematic because labeling the majority class requires labeling the minority class several times. In such cases, using methods like negative sampling or using synthetic data can help address these issues. This research explores the utilization of synthetic majority class data to enhance active learning. By generating this data using techniques like decision boundary augmentation, opposing sample generation, and generating samples based on the Manifold Mixup method, we can improve classification performance. According to our results, opposing sample generation yielded the best results in the US Postal Service dataset among the three synthetic methods. We've also compared this approach to standard active learning techniques and integrated it into a state-of-the-art semi-supervised active learning framework. Based on our results, combining opposing sample generation with the original method yielded significant improvements in classification performance and minimal increase in computation time. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of synthetic data to counter class imbalance

Nowadays, people can access the global network from any location, thereby minimizing the requirement for multiple physical sites. Moreover, the evolution of technologies like virtualization, protocols, and hypervisor has made it feasible to integrate numerous services onto a single network platform. 

  Despite these advancements, the issue of multiple protocols on a unified network still gives rise to compatibility issues, thus complicating the process of system integration. This problem has been accommodated to some extent through the development of higher-level standards, yet the task of vendor-independent service development remains a challenge. 

  To address this obstacle, we have developed a service-oriented architecture for host resource management that utilizes a resource bus, thereby allowing for independent service development while ensuring host availability and the observance of a common policy during service access. 

  Our architecture leverages the capabilities of Corba as its core, thereby providing a unified framework for creating and managing host resources and their distributed access through the implementation of the abstract service interface. 

  Implemented using Corba, our architecture comprises the Distributed Resource Object, the Resource Distribution Bus, and the Session Interface. A one-pass algorithm converging to the theoretical PCA solution has proven unfeasible due to the inability to estimate variances accurately in a single iteration. A commonly employed approach involves setting a threshold for the number of variances to consider, after which the eigenvalues converge to zero. However, this strategy results in compromised approximation quality. A recent research focused on developing a valuation function for suboptimal solutions in optimization problems as a possible solution to this issue. In this paper, we utilize this function to create two online PCA algorithms that can estimate principal vectors. We demonstrate the algorithms' ability to converge to the theoretical PCA solution in a single iteration and guarantee optimal approximation errors in the finite statistical model, outperforming previously established PCA algorithms based on valuation functions. Additionally, we extend our approach by incorporating the constraint of negative eigenvalues in the online non-convex PCA and study its practical effectiveness using real-world data, such as images from the CIFAR10 dataset, and medical diagnostic data for specific diseases. The results demonstrate our approach's ability to achieve comparable, if not superior, results compared to existing methods. A java-based source code for these algorithms is also provided. If ALPs decay into photons, they can emit additional radiation not accounted for by standard astrophysical models, leading to overestimated flux predictions and an apparent contradiction with the energy emitted by supernovae for certain ALP decay constants. However, we propose an alternative explanation: these supernovae might be experiencing persistent nuclear explosions triggered by the overexpansion of their outer shells. Consequently, the energy required to accommodate this gradient significantly surpasses the initial explosive energy. We observed this phenomenon in all core-collapse supernovae with sufficient data available and found evidence for prolonged activity in four such events: SN~1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, SN~2008S, SN~2009ip, and ASAS-SN 15am. A primary concern for these systems is the ability to trace a person's identity across different cameras without any prior knowledge. A new method, known as the Cross-domain Attention Network (CANet), has been developed to address this issue by creating a model capable of matching person images across different domains with high accuracy. CANet employs attention mechanisms to capture spatial features and generative adversarial networks to create realistic images from one domain that can be recognized in another. Preliminary experiments indicate that CANET delivers impressive results, achieving top-ranked performance on datasets such as the Market1501, CuHKface, and Bilinear ReID. Furthermore, the model is capable of performing cross-domain matching, outperforming existing approaches. A core strength of the network is its ability to extract distinct features from source domain images and distinguish between non-target images in the target domain through its dual attention mechanism, while a domain confusion module is used to counter bias and improve model robustness in cross-domain matching. Notably, the network can be easily adapted to work with cross-view scenarios by simply swapping the capture modes of the multi-channel input images. As an additional benefit, CANet also demonstrates strong real-world applicability, making it a highly suitable solution for the growing number of real-world surveillance systems on the rise. From an architectural perspective, CANet offers a wealth of possibilities for future improvements and can be integrated with various existing methods to enhance its performance and efficiency. From the experimental results, it is evident that CANet can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results when used on traditional ReID datasets. Following the established convention, we refer to neural-type models as NMTs, and traditional methods as CSMs (combinatorial search models). Like CSMS, NMTs are known as compression approaches for combinatorial search that utilize neural networks, are more closely related to Learning Augmenting Methods (LAM) [30], and deliver solution search via a form of compression. In this paper, we establish a four-fold equivalence between neural models and traditional compression methods for combinatorial search operationally. In other words, our study shows that CSMS can implement each of the four established compression approaches for combinatorial search, and conversely, NMTs can also execute these four approaches. Consequently, by combining NMTs' capabilities for learning features, filters, tableau modifications, and LAM in conjunction, our study leads to notable generalization performance and search efficiency improvements, mirroring prior research with symbolic models. Our findings are specifically validated in two domains known for their difficulty and complexity: non-deterministic finite state automaton minimization (NFSA) and maximum independent set search (MIS). Our study is the first to demonstrate NMT's efficacy in all four established compression approaches for combinatorial search, marking a crucial breakthrough in understanding the algorithmic essence of neural-type models in combinatorial search. We investigate stochastic processes on complex, self-similar networks known as Ramanujan networks, which have narrow degree distributions and numerous properties advantageous for analyzing network structure. However, calculating the topology of such networks is computationally expensive due to their large size and the intricate relationships between their components. We have discovered a new method to generate Ramanujan networks on any number of vertices with specific properties, providing a significant reduction in computational complexity and the ability to produce networks with a wide range of characteristics, such as varying edge cycles and irregularities. This technique enables us to establish a connection between network structure and stochastic processes, paving the way for a deeper understanding of stochastic processes and their relationship to real-world networks. The generated networks can serve as a reference point for testing various network analysis algorithms and modeling real-world networks. The ability to produce large Ramanujan networks gives us the opportunity to establish precise relationships between network properties and the likelihood of certain events occurring, such as the presence of short cycles. We have also shown that stochastic processes on such networks converge slowly and that this convergence is affected by the size of the neighborhoods when the networks have a bounded finite diameter. The properties of Ramanujan networks make them particularly useful for testing algorithms and models, and our work may lead to new applications in these areas. For instance, we have discovered a method to reconstruct a network's structure based on a stochastic process and neighborhood properties, and our simulations show that this method is effective on random networks. The main challenge of our approach is calculating the marginal probabilities needed for the process, and we have found a way to improve the accuracy of these calculations by utilizing a related process on a smaller grid and averaging the results. The geometric deep learning framework, widely adopted in artificial neural networks, lacks efficient and reliable methods for handling network cascades, specifically the spread of failures or epidemics within networks. To address this gap, our research establishes a framework using matrix and tensor factorizations that enable the transformation of these dynamics into a manageable set of parameters. By employing this approach, we demonstrate a faster rate of convergence and a simpler predictive model compared to the existing and commonly used degree-based model, with comparable accuracy. Additionally, our framework allows for the incorporation of numerous anisotropic (direction-dependent) and isotropic (direction-irrelevant) factors that may be present in various networks, and we illustrate its efficacy using three distinct scenarios: the spread of failures within a neural network, an epidemic within a human network, and a forest fire in a spatial network. Furthermore, our results also highlight the existence of a trade-off between model complexity and performance within these network cascades. The underlying framework can be adapted for use on graph datasets in general. Lastly, our research showcases an efficient and reliable method for accelerating convolutional operations on graph datasets, specifically by factorizing alternatingly coupled matrices and applying them as tensor products, which results in significant speedup (at least 5 times) when applied to a neural network convolution layer. Recent COD advancements primarily focus on the gray area between traditional object detection and camouflage, ignoring situations where objects are visually indistinguishable from their backgrounds. A robust COD solution must be capable of not only detecting objects that are partially visible but also those that are nearly indistinguishable from their surroundings. In an effort to address this underexplored area, we propose the creation of a new COD dataset called the Bayonet dataset which contains images of soldiers that are visually indistinguishable from their camouflage attire. A distinctive aspect of the Bayonet dataset is its focus on COD, which no longer relies solely on the traditional approach. Two cutting-edge Object Detection models, the Faster-RCNN and Bert-RCNN, are implemented and modified in order to tackle the VS COD challenge, respectively. The findings demonstrate that even highly advanced Object Detection models struggle with the VS COD challenge, highlighting the need for future improvements in this field. Ultimately, the proposed VS COD framework has the potential to refine COD methods by incorporating rigorous object disclosure assessments. A significant problem is accurately replicating lighting interactions between map objects and moving lights, yet current approaches significantly simplify this process. This research presents a new method for simulating the effects of dynamic light sources on high-DRI environment maps. Our approach, named EMapLighting, combines physical data and procedural techniques to replicate two types of light interactions: direct illumination and specular highlights. To handle direct illumination, EMapLighting captures the cast shadows of virtual objects and stores them as texture maps, while a soft rendering algorithm approximates the complex lighting interactions at occluded areas of the map. To simulate specular highlights, we created a new approximation of the micro-bump mapping effect, incorporating data from virtual object surfaces and using procedural algorithms to replicate the anatomy of map textures. Our results show that EMapLighting effectively advances the real-time rendering of high-DRI environment maps by accurately portraying both static and dynamic objects within these maps. Our technique is poised to facilitate innovative applications in real-time rendering, such as motion blur, tone mapping, and visualization of light scattering phenomena.
